opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the main reason is that these models learn from a very different kind of data than human biologists do, and at a very different scale.

A protein language model is trained on hundreds of millions of sequences, essentially the record of what evolution has produced across billions of years and every branch of life. Its training objective is simple: predict the masked or next amino acid. To do that well, it has to pick up on whatever regularities make a sequence plausible. Some of those regularities line up with things we already know: secondary structure, binding sites, contacts between residues that are far apart in sequence but close in 3D space. But nothing in the objective says "only learn the things humans have named." The model learns whatever is statistically useful, and evolution has encoded a lot of constraints we've never studied directly.

Our own documentation is also very uneven. Annotation in databases like UniProt is concentrated on a small fraction of well-studied proteins, often from a handful of model organisms, and it's organized around the concepts experimentalists could measure: a domain, an enzymatic activity, a localization signal. A huge amount of sequence space has never been characterized in a lab. So when we look inside these models, for example with sparse autoencoders or other interpretability methods that pull out individual features, some features map cleanly onto known annotations. Others are clearly coherent, firing consistently on a particular motif or structural context across unrelated protein families, but they don't match any label we have. They're more like latent concepts the model needed that we haven't gotten around to naming.

The question for the field is what those features actually are. Some may be real biology: subtle co-evolutionary patterns, physical constraints on folding or stability, or functional signals that cut across our existing categories. Some may be artifacts of how the training data was collected, such as sequencing biases or redundancy in the databases. So I'd be careful not to romanticize every unlabeled feature as a new discovery. But this is where interpretability becomes a scientific tool and not just a debugging tool. If we can find a feature the model reliably uses, form a hypothesis about it, and then test it in the lab, the model becomes a way of generating hypotheses about biology that we wouldn't have thought to ask.

So the short answer: the models are reading evolution's record more exhaustively than any human could, and our vocabulary of concepts was always shaped by what was easy for us to observe. The gap between those two is where these undocumented concepts live.

r001.rationale: It says annotations cover only a small fraction of proteins and much sequence space is uncharacterized, leaving model-learned concepts without human labels.

r002.rationale: It proposes using sparse autoencoders to pull out model features and describes some as coherent features that match no existing label.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that these models are trained on a very different kind of data than the data that produced our biology textbooks. Humans have characterized maybe a few thousand protein domains and motifs really carefully, and those are the ones we've written down and given names to. But the models are trained on hundreds of millions of sequences spanning the entire tree of life, and they're being optimized purely to predict what amino acid comes next, or what fills a masked position. To do that well, they have to pick up on whatever statistical regularities actually exist in evolution, whether or not a human has ever noticed or named them.

So when we actually go in and look at what the model is representing, we do find the familiar stuff. There are features that light up for well-known things like zinc fingers or transmembrane helices or particular binding sites. That's the reassuring part, because it tells you the model is learning real biology. But then there's this other set of features that fire very consistently on specific structural or sequence patterns, and when we go to the literature, there's just no corresponding concept. Nobody has written a paper about it. And some of these look like they're capturing something meaningful, like a motif associated with a particular fold or a conserved region that shows up across families.

My interpretation is that this isn't really surprising if you think about it. Human biology is bottlenecked by what individual researchers happened to study, what was experimentally tractable, what got funded. The model doesn't have those biases. It just sees the data. So there's a real opportunity here, which is that interpretability isn't only about auditing the model or making sure it's behaving the way we want. It can actually be a discovery tool. The model has, in some sense, read more biology than any person ever could, and if we can learn to translate what it has internalized, we can get new hypotheses out of it. That's one of the things I find most exciting about this direction.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the few thousand carefully characterized protein domains and motifs with models trained on hundreds of millions of sequences, and says human study is limited by research choices and experimental tractability.

r002.rationale: The response describes interpretability as a potential discovery tool, but does not mention sparse autoencoders or propose investigating whether SAEs can extract undocumented concepts.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that protein language models learn directly from a huge number of protein sequences, rather than from our descriptions of how proteins work. Those sequences reflect evolutionary constraints: a protein has to fold, it has to interact with other molecules, and often it has to perform a very specific function. So there’s a lot of structure in that data that we haven’t fully characterized as humans.

When we look inside these models, we can find features that correspond to concepts we already know, like particular structural elements or functional regions. That gives us some confidence that the representations are capturing meaningful biology. But we also find features that consistently pick out patterns across proteins without matching an existing annotation.

Now, that doesn’t automatically mean the model has discovered a new biological concept. It could be a statistical artifact, or something we know about but haven’t annotated well. The exciting possibility is that these features give us hypotheses: here’s a pattern the model finds useful, here are the proteins where it appears, and now we can design experiments to understand what it does.

r001.rationale: The response says protein sequence patterns are not fully characterized by humans and that some model features do not match existing annotations, identifying incomplete human annotation as a reason.

r002.rationale: The response proposes investigating model features through experiments, but it does not mention sparse autoencoders (SAEs) or propose using them to extract undocumented concepts.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’d frame that as a hypothesis rather than something we can simply assume. These models are trained on enormous numbers of protein sequences, and those sequences reflect evolutionary constraints. For a protein to function, different parts of its sequence often need to work together. So predicting which amino acids belong in a sequence can require learning something about structure and function, even without explicit labels for those properties.

Human annotations cover only a small fraction of that information. We’ve experimentally studied a relatively small subset of proteins, and our descriptions tend to focus on categories we already know to look for. The model doesn’t have that same restriction. It can pick up recurring patterns that we haven’t named or investigated yet.

But finding a pattern in a model isn’t enough to establish a new biological concept. The exciting step is turning that pattern into a testable hypothesis: can we change a sequence in a way the model predicts and then observe the corresponding change in the protein? That’s where we can start connecting what the model has learned to new scientific understanding.

r001.rationale: It says human annotations cover only a small fraction of protein information, while models can learn recurring unnamed patterns from sequence data.

r002.rationale: It does not mention sparse autoencoders or propose using them to extract undocumented concepts.
